title: Never the fruit, never careless
hookLine: the numbers are down, and two people quote the same book: stop counting, or count everything
carry: let go of the fruit, never the consequences
tomorrow: the Gita names a heat a reviewer should let go of. what is it?

cards: The food drive's numbers are in, and they're down from last year. Around the table, two people start talking at once. One says: stop counting.
We did it for the right reasons, and the Gita says the fruit isn't ours. The other says: count everything. If fewer families ate, we need to know why.
Both of them are leaning on the same book.

teach.b: Hear the first view at its best. In chapter two, Krishna says, in paraphrase: your concern is the action, never its fruit; don't let the fruit be your reason. A review that lives on numbers starts working for the numbers.

The volunteer who reads with one slow kid all year looks bad on a chart. Counting can turn service into a scoreboard, and the Gita warns against exactly that grasping. Now the second view at its best.

teach.h: NO REGARD FOR CONSEQUENCE: THE DARK KIND.
teach.b: In chapter eighteen, Krishna sorts actions into three kinds, and the dark kind is begun in confusion, without regard for consequence, for loss, for harm, or for one's own strength.
The Sanskrit for consequence there is anubandha, what follows on. Ignoring results isn't freedom on that list. It's a mark of the darkest action.
If the drive fed fewer families, somebody went without, and not looking is its own carelessness. Some readers put the weight on letting go. Some put it on paying attention.
Both start from the same book. And the two lines can sit side by side. What chapter two warns against is grasping at the fruit for oneself: was I thanked, did I look good?
Chapter eighteen's list asks about others and about strength: what came of it, what did it cost, did it harm anyone, was it within reach?
That's nishkama karma, action without craving for its fruit, read whole: let go of the credit, keep your eyes on what the action does.

teach.h: LET GO OF THE FRUIT, NEVER THE CONSEQUENCES.
teach.b: And it's the fourth design rule, the review.

how: Hindu teachers read Gita 2.47 and 18.23–25 together when they speak about service: act without grasping at the fruit, yet stay responsible for what the action does to others.

o: action judged only by the thanks it earns
action that matters only for its intentions
action reviewed for what it did for others

games.q: one book, two views — tap the pairs.
p: no regard for consequence or harm
stop counting, or you'll work for the count
not looking is its own carelessness

s: the Gita says results never matter at all
chapter eighteen calls action begun without regard for consequence, loss or harm the dark kind.
in chapter two, Krishna says your concern is the action, not its fruit
and don't let the fruit be your reason.
chapter eighteen's questions are about what the doer gets out of it
consequence, cost, harm and one's own strength; credit isn't on the list.

games.q: you tutor a kid every week. his grades haven't moved, but he finally reads aloud without freezing. a friend says, 'then it isn't working.' what does chapter eighteen's review ask?
o: what came of it for him, including what's hard to graph.
only whether his grades went up this term.
nothing. the Gita says not to look at results.
games.why: the dark action ignores what follows; the clear review looks at consequence, cost, harm and strength. a kid who can read aloud is a consequence too.

practice: Bring to mind one thing you did for someone this month. Softly, out loud if you can, ask it the four questions, one on each slow breath: what came of it, what did it cost, did it harm anyone, was it within my strength.
Then let the answers sit, with no score attached.

wordCard.voice: Karma, under review: what came of it, what it cost, any harm, and whether it fit your strength. No scoreboard of credit.

orig.note: Sanskrit anubandha, consequence, what follows on from an act; Gita 18.25 names ignoring it as a mark of the dark action.

carryVoice: The line, straight from the Gita: let go of the fruit, never the consequences. Day five of seven.

sources.ref: Bhagavad Gita 2.47 (your concern is the action, never its fruits; don't let the fruit be the motive, nor cling to inaction)

Bhagavad Gita 18.23–25 (sattvic action done as it should be, without attachment, by one not seeking the fruit; rajasic action done with strain, for desires or from ego; tamasic action begun from delusion without regard to consequence, loss, harm or one's own capacity)
